blocks.p: Now, when they had nearly come out of this wilderness, Faithful happened to look back and saw someone coming after them, and he knew him.
“Oh!” said Faithful to his brother. “Who’s that coming?”
Christian looked and said, “It’s my good friend Evangelist.”
“Yes, and my good friend too,” said Faithful, “for it was he who set me on the way to the gate.”
Now Evangelist came up to them and greeted them.
“Peace be with you, dearly loved friends, and peace to those who help you.”
“Welcome, welcome, my good Evangelist,” said Christian. “The sight of your face brings back to me all your old kindness and your tireless work for my eternal good.”
“And a thousand times welcome,” said good Faithful. “O sweet Evangelist, how much your company means to us poor pilgrims!”
“How has it gone with you, my friends, since we last parted?” said Evangelist. “What have you met with, and how have you conducted yourselves?”
Then Christian and Faithful told him everything that had happened to them on the way, and how, and with what difficulty, they had arrived at that place.

“I am very glad,” said Evangelist, “not that you have met with trials, but that you have come through them victorious, and that, in spite of many weaknesses, you have kept to the way to this very day.

“I say, I am very glad of it, both for my own sake and for yours. I sowed, and you have reaped; and the day is coming when the one who sowed and those who reaped will rejoice together, that is, if you hold out; ‘for at the proper time you will reap, if you do not give up.’ [John 4:36; Gal. 6:9] The crown is in front of you, and it is a crown that will never perish; so run in such a way that you win it. [1 Cor. 9:24-27] There are some who set out for this crown, and after they have gone a long way toward it, someone else comes in and takes it from them. So hold on to what you have, so that no one takes your crown. [Rev. 3:11] You are not yet out of the devil’s range. You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood in your struggle against sin. Keep the kingdom always before you, and believe steadfastly in the things that are unseen. Let nothing on this side of the other world get inside you. Above all, keep careful watch over your own hearts and their desires, ‘for the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked.’ Set your faces like flint. You have all power in heaven and on earth on your side.”

Christian thanked him for his encouragement, but told him that they wanted him to speak further, to help them for the rest of the way, especially since they knew he was a prophet and could tell them what might happen to them, and how they might resist and overcome it. Faithful joined in the request. So Evangelist began.

“My sons, you have heard in the true words of the gospel that you must pass through many troubles to enter the kingdom of heaven; and again, that in every city chains and hardships are waiting for you. So you cannot expect to go far on your pilgrimage without them, in one form or another. You have already found something of the truth of this, and more is about to follow. For now, as you see, you are almost out of this wilderness, and soon you will come to a town that you will see ahead of you. In that town you will be fiercely beset by enemies, who will strain every nerve to kill you. And you may be sure that one or both of you must seal the testimony you hold with your blood. But be faithful to death, and the King will give you the crown of life.

“Whichever of you dies there, though his death will be unnatural and his pain perhaps great, will have the better part. Not only will he arrive at the Celestial City sooner, but he will escape many miseries that the other will meet with in the rest of his journey. But when you come to the town and find that what I have told you has come true, then remember your friend, and acquit yourselves like men, and commit the keeping of your souls to your God by doing good, as to a faithful Creator.”

Then I saw in my dream that when they had come out of the wilderness, they soon saw a town ahead of them. The name of that town is Vanity, and in the town there is a fair, called Vanity Fair, which is kept all year round. It bears the name Vanity Fair because the town where it is held is lighter than vanity itself, and because everything sold there, or that comes there, is vanity. As the wise man says, “All that comes is vanity.” [Eccl. 1; 2:11, 17; 11:8; Isa. 11:17]
This fair is no new business; it is a thing of ancient standing. I will tell you how it began.

Almost five thousand years ago, there were pilgrims walking to the Celestial City, just as these two honest men are. Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion, with their companions, saw from the path the pilgrims had worn that their way to the city ran through this town of Vanity; and so they planned to set up a fair here, a fair where every kind of vanity would be sold, and which would last all year long. And so at this fair all sorts of merchandise are sold: houses, lands, trades, positions, honors, promotions, titles, countries, kingdoms, lusts, pleasures, and delights of every kind; prostitutes and pimps, wives, husbands, children, masters, servants, lives, blood, bodies, souls, silver, gold, pearls, precious stones, and what not.
At this fair, moreover, there are always to be seen swindlers, games, plays, fools, apes, cheats, and rogues of every kind.
Here, too, can be seen, and for free, thefts, murders, adulteries, and perjurers, and those of a blood-red color.

And just as other, lesser fairs have their rows and streets under their proper names, where this or that kind of goods is sold, so here too you have the proper places, rows, and streets, that is, countries and kingdoms, where the wares of this fair are most easily found. Here is Britain Row, French Row, Italian Row, Spanish Row, German Row, where all sorts of vanities are sold. And as in other fairs some one commodity is the chief of the whole fair, so the goods of Rome and her merchandise are heavily promoted at this fair; only our English nation, along with some others, has taken a dislike to them.

Now, as I said, the way to the Celestial City runs right through this town where this lusty fair is held, and anyone who wants to go to the city without going through this town would have to go out of the world. [1 Cor. 5:10] The Prince of princes himself, when he was here, went through this town on the way to his own country, and on a fair day, too. Indeed, as I understand it, it was Beelzebub, the chief lord of this fair, who invited him to buy his vanities; he would even have made him lord of the fair if only he would bow down to him as he passed through the town. [Matt. 4:8; Luke 4:5-7] Because he was a person of such honor, Beelzebub took him from street to street and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, to see if he could tempt the Blessed One to haggle over and buy some of his vanities. But he had no interest in the merchandise, and so he left the town without spending so much as a penny on these vanities. This fair, then, is an ancient thing, of long standing, and a very great fair.

Now these pilgrims, as I said, had to go through this fair. And so they did. But as soon as they entered the fair, all the people in it were stirred up, and the whole town was in an uproar over them, for several reasons.

First, the pilgrims were dressed in clothing different from that of anyone who traded in the fair. So the people of the fair stared at them. Some said they were fools, some that they were lunatics, and some that they were strange foreigners. [1 Cor. 2:7-8]

Second, just as they marveled at their clothing, so they marveled at their speech, for few could understand what they said. The pilgrims naturally spoke the language of Canaan, but those who kept the fair were men of this world; so from one end of the fair to the other, each seemed a barbarian to the other.

Third, what puzzled the merchants most was that these pilgrims thought very little of all their goods. They did not care even to look at them, and when the merchants called on them to buy, they would put their fingers in their ears and cry, “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things,” and look upward, signifying that their trade and business was in heaven. [Ps. 119:37; Phil. 3:19-20]
One man, watching the way they carried themselves, happened to say to them mockingly, “What will you buy?”
They looked at him gravely and answered, “We buy the truth.” [Prov. 23:23]

That gave the people an excuse to despise them all the more. Some mocked, some taunted, some spoke insultingly, and some called on others to hit them. At last there was such an uproar and commotion in the fair that all order broke down. Word was quickly brought to the great one of the fair, who came down at once and appointed some of his most trusted friends to examine these men over whom the fair had nearly been turned upside down.

So the men were brought in for examination, and those who sat in judgment on them asked where they came from, where they were going, and what they were doing there in such unusual dress. The men told them that they were pilgrims and strangers in the world, and that they were going to their own country, which was the heavenly Jerusalem [Heb. 11:13-16]; and that they had given the people of the town and the merchants no reason to abuse them like this and hinder them on their journey, unless it was that when someone asked them what they would buy, they said they would buy the truth. But those appointed to examine them did not believe they were anything but lunatics and madmen, or else men who had come to throw the whole fair into confusion. So they took them and beat them, smeared them with filth, and then put them in the cage, to make them a spectacle to everyone at the fair.

v: Behold Vanity Fair! The pilgrims there
and so our Lord once passed through here,

blocks.p: There they lay for some time, made the object of any man’s sport, or spite, or revenge, while the great one of the fair laughed at everything that happened to them. But the men were patient, and did not return insult for insult. On the contrary, they gave blessing, and good words for bad, and kindness for injuries. And so some people in the fair who were more observant and less prejudiced than the rest began to restrain and rebuke the baser sort for their constant abuse of the men. These turned on them angrily, counting them as bad as the men in the cage, saying they looked like accomplices and should share their punishment. The others replied that, as far as they could see, the men were quiet and sober and meant no one any harm, and that there were many who traded in their fair who deserved the cage, and the pillory too, far more than the men they had abused.

So, after many words had passed on both sides, while the two men behaved very wisely and soberly before them all, the townspeople came to blows among themselves and did one another harm. Then these two poor men were brought before their examiners again and charged with being guilty of the recent uproar in the fair. So they beat them pitilessly, put irons on them, and led them in chains up and down the fair, as an example and a terror to others, so that no one would speak for them or join them.

But Christian and Faithful behaved more wisely still, and received the disgrace and shame heaped on them with such meekness and patience that they won several of the men of the fair to their side, though only a few compared with the rest. This put the other party in an even greater rage, so much so that they resolved on the death of these two men. They threatened that neither the cage nor the irons would be enough, but that they should die for the harm they had done and for deceiving the men of the fair.
Then they were sent back to the cage until further orders could be given. So they put them in, and fastened their feet in the stocks.

Here they called to mind again what they had heard from their faithful friend Evangelist, and were strengthened all the more in their way and their sufferings by the fact that he had told them it would happen. They also comforted each other that whichever of them was chosen to suffer would have the better part; and so each man secretly wished that the honor might be his. But committing themselves to the all-wise will of Him who rules all things, they stayed contentedly in the condition they were in, until other arrangements should be made for them.
